## PROP  
 38

## AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH. INITIATIVE STATUTE.

### SUMMARY

### Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures

Authorizes $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, half to a single University of California-affiliated nonprofit medical research institute, half to research grants. **Fiscal Impact:** Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years to repay the research bond, with some or all of the cost offset if the funded research generates revenue. **Supporters:** Michael J. Fox Foundation; Alzheimer’s Los Angeles; Kidney Cancer Assoc; American Nurses Assoc\\CA **Opponents:** Robert M Kaplan Ph.D.

### WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS

YES A YES vote on this measure means: The state could borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.

NO A NO vote on this measure means: The state could not borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.

 

### ARGUMENTS

PRO YES on 38 supports life-saving immunology research to cure and prevent diseases like cancer, heart disease, Alzheimer’s. Strong accountability including independent audits. Mandates 20% Rx discount. Designed to ensure no cost to taxpayers. YES on 38 could save your life and someone you love. Alzheimer’s Association, The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research urge YES on 38!  
 www.YESon38.com

CON California should continue supporting biomedical research, but Proposition 38 is the wrong approach. It would commit taxpayers to decades of new bond debt while limiting California’s flexibility to address changing health priorities. Research funding should be guided through the normal budget process—not by ballot initiatives.

## PROP  
 38

## AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH. INITIATIVE STATUTE.

## ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST

### BACKGROUND

***Medical Research and Development (R&D) Is a Multi- Stage Process.*** The first stage of this process is basic research, which focuses on discovering new knowledge about how the human body works. The next stage is applied and clinical research, which aims to develop and test treatments for specific diseases. Universities do most of the basic research, while companies do most of the applied and clinical research. The third R&D stage is to have regulators review new treatments to make sure they are safe and effective. If a new treatment is approved, then it may be used on patients. Most R&D projects do not make it through all of these stages.

***Medical R&D Is Funded in Various Ways.*** Funding for medical R&D in the United States totaled about $300 billion in 2023. Companies and government agencies (such as the National Institutes of Health) are the major funding sources for R&D nationally and in California. Beyond these funding sources, California voters have approved two ballot measures— Proposition 71 (2004) and Proposition 14 (2020)— giving the state authority to issue general obligation bonds to fund specified medical research. Combined, the two measures allowed the state to issue $8.5 billion in bonds for stem cell research. Bonds are a way for the state to borrow money, then repay it with interest over time. A general obligation bond is typically repaid from the state General Fund. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.) For more information about bonds, see “Overview of State Bond Debt” later in this guide.

### PROPOSAL

***New Bond for Specified Medical Research.*** Proposition 38 allows the state to issue an $8.4 billion general obligation bond for research in immunology and immunotherapy. Immunology is the study of the body’s immune system and how it protects the body from abnormal cells and other causes of disease. Immunotherapy develops treatments that help the immune system fight diseases more effectively. The measure requires that at least $4.2 billion of the bond funds be used for immunology research on cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s disease. No more than 2 percent of total bond funds may be used for state administrative costs. Payments on the bond would come from the state General Fund.

***Supports a Research Institute.*** About half of the bond funds would go to a research institute specializing in immunology and immunotherapy. The California Department of Public Health (CDPH) would select the institute. The selected institute must meet several criteria, including criteria related to its size, funding, and collaboration with a University of California (UC) campus. The institute would use the bond funds for research. Each year, the institute must issue a public report on its activities and have an independent financial audit.

***Supports Research Grants.*** A council would give out the other half of bond funds as competitive research grants focused on immunology and immunotherapy. The council would consist of representatives from 7 UC campuses and 10 to 15 other universities and nonprofit research institutions in California. The council would set research priorities and select grant recipients from among its member organizations. Similar to the institute, the council would have public reporting and audit requirements.

***Requires 10 Percent of Revenue From Discoveries First Be Used to Repay the State.*** Proposition 38 requires that the institute, in consultation with CDPH, try to generate the most revenue possible from the funded research. (Research, for example, could lead to the development of a new medical treatment.) Ten percent of any revenue generated must be given to the state. This revenue must first go into the state General Fund until it repays the cost of the research bond (the amount borrowed plus the interest). Any additional revenue would be used for future immunology and immunotherapy research.

***Has Two Other Notable Provisions.*** 

*   ***Requires Purchases From California Suppliers.*** Grant recipients must buy at least half of their goods and services from California suppliers when reasonably possible.
*   ***Requires California Patient Discount.*** Any treatment developed through funded research and sold in California must generally be offered at a 20 percent discount.

### FISCAL EFFECTS

***Increased State Cost of $500 Million to $600 Million Annually for About 20 Years to Repay the Bond.*** The state General Fund cost to repay the bond would be **$500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years**. The annual cost would be about one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Since the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, the total cost of the bond would be about 10 percent more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up-front with money it already has.

***Potential State Revenue From Research Discoveries.*** The state could receive revenue from research funded by Proposition 38. The amount of revenue is uncertain but could be significant. It would depend on how many research projects lead to marketable treatments and how much money any given treatment generates. The timing of these revenues and how long it would take to offset the state’s bond cost is also uncertain, but could take decades.

***Potential Indirect Fiscal Effects.*** Proposition 38 likely would have some indirect fiscal effects, particularly on costs for state health programs (such as Medi-Cal, which pays for health care for low-income Californians). For example, if the funded research leads to new medical treatments, the average cost of patient care could either increase or decrease. As a result, the overall effect on program costs is uncertain.

### REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 38

California should continue supporting biomedical research. Everyone hopes for new treatments for heart disease, cancer, Alzheimer’s disease, and other serious illnesses. I do too. But Proposition 38 is the wrong way to achieve that goal.

The claim that Proposition 38 will pay for itself is speculative. Audits, public disclosure, and limits on administrative costs promote accountability, but they cannot guarantee that research investments will generate enough economic returns to offset billions of dollars in bond repayments.

California faces a continuing structural budget deficit.

Proposition 38 would require approximately $8.4 billion in bond repayments. According to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, taxpayers would be committed to roughly $500 million in annual debt payments for the next 25 years. That long-term obligation would further reduce the state’s fiscal flexibility to respond to changing priorities.

Meanwhile, recent actions by the Trump administration have placed funding for essential California public health programs at risk, including disease surveillance, emergency preparedness, HIV prevention, vaccination infrastructure, laboratory capacity, and community prevention. These challenges extend well beyond biomedical research.

If California chooses to replace declining federal support, elected officials should be able to consider all health priorities together. Proposition 38 instead earmarks billions of borrowed dollars for one scientific field, regardless of future needs or discoveries. Research priorities should be guided through the normal budget process—not by ballot measures that lock taxpayers into decades of debt. Vote No on Proposition 38.

**Robert M Kaplan**, Ph.D.

### ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 38

California recognizes that continued investment in science is essential. But this proposition is not the best way to achieve that goal.

The measure would authorize approximately $8.4 billion in state borrowing to support immunology and immunotherapy research through a new University of California institute. Although the objective is appealing, the financing and policy framework are flawed.

First, the proposition continues the use of ballot initiatives to direct research funding toward selected topics. California has already created separate funding programs for stem cell research and precision medicine. This measure would add another highly focused program. Research priorities should be established through scientific review and public health planning—not by election campaigns. Cancer, Alzheimer’s disease, and heart disease deserve attention, but so do mental illness, kidney disease, eye diseases, and many other conditions. Ballot-box science inevitably favors the most visible topics rather than the greatest scientific opportunities or public health needs.

Second, borrowing is an inappropriate way to finance scientific research. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the bonds authorized by this measure would obligate taxpayers to $500 million in annual debt payments for about 25 years. Bonds are commonly used for highways, schools, and other long-lived infrastructure with predictable benefits. Scientific research is different. Discoveries often require decades before they improve patient care, and many promising lines of investigation never produce marketable treatments.

Third, the proposition assumes that successful discoveries will generate revenues to offset state costs. In reality, universities rarely commercialize new therapies on their own. Publicly funded research lays the scientific foundation, but private companies typically invest the far greater resources required for product development, clinical testing, manufacturing, and regulatory approval. The public benefits are real, but they generally do not flow back to the state treasury.

Finally, the proposition requires certain therapies developed with state support to be sold in California at discounted prices. While this may sound attractive, it could incentivize companies to prioritize selling these products in other states where the prices are not controlled.

California should continue to support biomedical research. But research funding should be strategic, flexible, and fiscally responsible. Decisions about scientific priorities should be based on expert evaluation of emerging scientific opportunities and public health needs, not on a series of expensive ballot measures financed through long-term debt.

California has better options. For example, Senator Scott Wiener has proposed creating a state-funded research agency modeled on the National Institutes of Health and the National Science Foundation. Rather than directing resources to specific areas of science, such an institution could establish priorities through expert scientific review and adapt its investments as new opportunities emerge. Although the legislation has not advanced, it received support from the University of California, the United Auto Workers, and the Union of American Physicians and Dentists. Similar legislation is likely to be considered in the future.

A “No” vote does not reject science. It rejects an inefficient financing mechanism and a fragmented approach to setting research priorities. California can and should support medical research through more coordinated, sustainable policies.

**Robert M Kaplan**, Ph.D.

# **Proposition 38**

Authorizes Bonds for Immunology Medical Research. Initiative Statute.

## Analysis of Measure

### Background

***Medical Research and Development (R&D) Is a Multi-Stage Process.*** The first stage of this process is basic research, which focuses on discovering new knowledge about how the human body works. The next stage is applied and clinical research, which aims to develop and test treatments for specific diseases. Universities do most of the basic research, while companies do most of the applied and clinical research. The third R&D stage is to have regulators review new treatments to make sure they are safe and effective. If a new treatment is approved, then it may be used on patients. Most R&D projects do not make it through all of these stages.

***Medical R&D Is Funded in Various Ways.*** Funding for medical R&D in the United States totaled about $300 billion in 2023. Companies and government agencies (such as the National Institutes of Health) are the major funding sources for R&D nationally and in California. Beyond these funding sources, California voters have approved two ballot measures—Proposition 71 (2004) and Proposition 14 (2020)—giving the state authority to issue general obligation bonds to fund specified medical research. Combined, the two measures allowed the state to issue $8.5 billion in bonds for stem cell research. Bonds are a way for the state to borrow money, then repay it with interest over time. A general obligation bond is typically repaid from the state General Fund. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.) For more information about bonds, see “Overview of State Bond Debt” later in this guide.

### Proposal

***New Bond for Specified Medical Research.*** Proposition 38 allows the state to issue an $8.4 billion general obligation bond for research in immunology and immunotherapy. Immunology is the study of the body’s immune system and how it protects the body from abnormal cells and other causes of disease. Immunotherapy develops treatments that help the immune system fight diseases more effectively. The measure requires that at least $4.2 billion of the bond funds be used for immunology research on cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s disease. No more than 2 percent of total bond funds may be used for state administrative costs. Payments on the bond would come from the state General Fund.

***Supports a Research Institute.*** About half of the bond funds would go to a research institute specializing in immunology and immunotherapy. The California Department of Public Health (CDPH) would select the institute. The selected institute must meet several criteria, including criteria related to its size, funding, and collaboration with a University of California (UC) campus. The institute would use the bond funds for research. Each year, the institute must issue a public report on its activities and have an independent financial audit.

***Supports Research Grants.*** A council would give out the other half of bond funds as competitive research grants focused on immunology and immunotherapy. The council would consist of representatives from 7 UC campuses and 10 to 15 other universities and nonprofit research institutions in California. The council would set research priorities and select grant recipients from among its member organizations. Similar to the institute, the council would have public reporting and audit requirements.

***Requires 10 Percent of Revenue From Discoveries First Be Used to Repay the State.*** Proposition 38 requires that the institute, in consultation with CDPH, try to generate the most revenue possible from the funded research. (Research, for example, could lead to the development of a new medical treatment.) Ten percent of any revenue generated must be given to the state. This revenue must first go into the state General Fund until it repays the cost of the research bond (the amount borrowed plus the interest). Any additional revenue would be used for future immunology and immunotherapy research.

***Has Two Other Notable Provisions.*** 

*   ***Requires Purchases From California Suppliers.*** Grant recipients must buy at least half of their goods and services from California suppliers when reasonably possible.
*   ***Requires California Patient Discount.*** Any treatment developed through funded research and sold in California must generally be offered at a 20 percent discount.

### Fiscal Effects

***Increased State Cost of $500 Million to $600 Million Annually for About 20 Years to Repay the Bond.*** The state General Fund cost to repay the bond would be **$500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years**. The annual cost would be about one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Since the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, the total cost of the bond would be about 10 percent more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up-front with money it already has.

***Potential State Revenue From Research Discoveries.*** The state could receive revenue from research funded by Proposition 38. The amount of revenue is uncertain but could be significant. It would depend on how many research projects lead to marketable treatments and how much money any given treatment generates. The timing of these revenues and how long it would take to offset the state’s bond cost is also uncertain, but could take decades.

***Potential Indirect Fiscal Effects.*** Proposition 38 likely would have some indirect fiscal effects, particularly on costs for state health programs (such as Medi-Cal, which pays for health care for low-income Californians). For example, if the funded research leads to new medical treatments, the average cost of patient care could either increase or decrease. As a result, the overall effect on program costs is uncertain.

* * *

## Yes/No Statement

A **YES** vote on this measure means: The state could borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.

A **NO** vote on this measure means: The state could not borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.

* * *

## Summary of Legislative Analyst’s Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact

*   Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years to repay the medical research bond. The state could recover part or all of this cost in subsequent decades if the funded research leads to discoveries that generate revenue.

**Fiscal Impact**: Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years to repay the research bond, with some or all of the cost offset if the funded research generates revenue.

 **California Proposition 38**, the **Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Funding Initiative**, is on the [ballot](/California_2026_ballot_propositions "California 2026 ballot propositions") in [California](/California "California") as an [initiated state statute](/Initiated_state_statute "Initiated state statute") on [November 3, 2026](/California_2026_ballot_propositions "California 2026 ballot propositions").[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

A "**yes**" vote supports an initiative to:

*   authorize the state to issue $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds to fund immunology and immunotherapy research;
*   require the state to enter a partnership with an immunology and immunotherapy research institute affiliated with the University of California and allocate half of the bond revenue to that research institute; and
*   use the remaining funds for grants to California-based public and nonprofit medical research institutions for immunology and immunotherapy research.

A "**no**" vote opposes this initiative to issue $8.4 billion in bonds to fund research and development treatments using immunology and immunotherapy.

## Overview

### What would Proposition 38 do?

*See also: [Measure design](#Measure_design)*

Proposition 38 would issue $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds to fund immunology and immunotherapy research. The initiative would require at least $4.2 billion in bond revenue to be used for research related to cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer's disease. The initiative would also authorize the state to enter into an agreement with a nonprofit institute dedicated to researching immunology and immunotherapy within 90 days of the effective date of the initiative. Half of the bond revenue after deducting administrative costs would be allocated to the designated institute. The initiative would allocate the remaining bond revenue to public and nonprofit universities or medical research institutes through a competitive grant process.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

### What would the criteria be for the grant process?

*See also: [Measure design](#Measure_design)*

The initiative would establish an Advisory and Accountability Research Council authorized to set research priorities and establish the criteria for the grant process. The council would consider the scientific merits of the proposal, the medical research experience of the applicant, the potential benefits to the health of the population, and other criteria established by the council when considering proposals.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

The initiative would require grant recipients to own any intellectual property created from the research, meaning employees, scientists, researchers, contractors, or anyone paid with the grant would be required to formally assign their patent or intellectual property rights to the institution receiving the funding. It would also require grant recipients that currently own or license older technology or patents that could limit the use or selling of the products created by the research to grant a worldwide, royalty-free license for the older technology so that the new products or inventions can be created and sold.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

### Who supports and opposes Proposition 38?

*See also: [Support](#Support) and [Opposition](#Opposition)*

[YES on 38: Californians for Life-Saving Immunology Research and Cures](#Support) is leading the campaign in support of Proposition 38. It has received endorsements from ALS Association, Alzheimer’s Association, American Nurses Association of California, California Black Health Network, Michelson Center for Public Policy, and Parkinson Association of Northern California. YES on the California Immunology Research & Cures Initiative campaign said, "California has an opportunity to accelerate lifesaving medical breakthroughs. Immunotherapies work differently than traditional treatments. Instead of attacking cells directly, they empower the body’s own immune system to recognize and stop disease. Today, these therapies are already treating certain cancers and chronic conditions — and researchers continue to expand what’s possible. This initiative invests in proven science so cures can move from the lab to patients faster."[\[2\]](#cite_note-support-2) 

[No on Proposition 38](#Opposition) is leading the campaign in opposition to Proposition 38. It has received endorsements from the League of Women Voters California and Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association.[\[3\]](#cite_note-oppose-3) Dr. Robert Kaplan, a senior scholar at the Clinical Excellence Research Center at the Stanford School of Medicine who opposes the initiative, said, "As written, Proposition 38 is deceptive. It will funnel billions of dollars to benefit its billionaire donor. Voters should reject a measure that channels half of the state funds to one institution based on arbitrary criteria chosen by the proposition authors. Grants for medical research should be awarded through a competitive process that gives all competitors an equal chance."[\[4\]](#cite_note-4)

Bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research

The initiative would authorize the state to issue $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds to fund immunology and immunotherapy research. The initiative would require at least $4.2 billion in bond revenue to be used for research related to cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer's disease. The initiative would also limit state administrative costs to 2%. Bond revenue and other revenue generated from the research, such as license, royalties, or other income, would be deposited into a new fund, the California Immunology and Immunotherapy Medical Research Fund.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)

  
 The initiative would require the selected institute described below to develop a licensing program to maximize revenues from the funded research. It would require the first 10% of any income generated by the research, such as license, royalties, or other income, from the selected institute or other grantees to be deposited into the state's General Fund to repay the costs of the bonds. Following the repayment of the bonds, the first 10% would be deposited into a new fund, the California Immunology and Immunotherapy Medical Research Fund.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)  
 

The initiative would require that technology, treatments, or drug development resulting from funded research be discounted for California patients by 20%.

State partnership with immunology and immunotherapy nonprofit institute

The initiative would authorize the state to enter into an agreement with a nonprofit institute dedicated to researching immunology and immunotherapy within 90 days of the effective date of the initiative. The medical institute would be selected by the California Department of Public Health (CDPH) and meet the following criteria:[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)

*   specialize in immunology and immunotherapy;
*   exempt from federal income tax that was operating prior to January 1, 2025;
*   has an affiliation agreement with a campus of the University of California that has a graduate program in the related field, a public healthcare system with at least one hospital that conducts its own clinical trials, and the public healthcare system has a hospital/clinic volume of at least 35,000 inpatient admissions and 3.5 million outpatient visits each year;
*   governed by a board of directors that includes multiple members who are senior-level representatives of the University of California-affiliated campus;
*   owns or leases a site not less than 200,000 square feet in size for research activities;
*   agrees to conduct collaborative research with other qualified nonprofit California medical research centers;
*   receives at least $25 million from philanthropic donations; and
*   secured financial commitments of at least $50 million each for a rapid vaccine development program and microbiome research program.

  
 

Half of the bond revenue after deducting administrative costs would be allocated to the designated institute. CDPH would be required to review that the institute has complied with the agreement every five years.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)

Competitive grants for public and nonprofit universities and medical research institutes

The initiative would allocate the remaining bond revenue to public and nonprofit universities or medical research institutes through a competitive grant process. The initiative would establish an Advisory and Accountability Research Council authorized to set research priorities and establish the criteria for the grant process. The council would consist of seven executive committee members appointed by the chancellors of the University of California campuses at Berkeley, Davis, Irvine, Los Angeles, Riverside, San Diego, and San Francisco. The seven executive members would then appoint between 10 and 15 additional members by majority vote. The members must be representatives of California nonprofit universities and representatives of state medical research institutes with demonstrated success in immunology and immunotherapy research. Members of the council would also be required to be a doctor, scientist, or researcher and serve four-year terms.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)

  
 The initiative would authorize grants based on the following:[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

*   the scientific merits of the proposal,
*   the medical research experience of the applicant,
*   the potential benefits to the health of the population, and
*   other criteria established by the council.

  
 Council members would be excluded from the review process if they are on a scientific peer review panel and have a collaborative or commercial relationship with the applicant. Grants would be awarded to state-based researchers, with exceptions for collaborations between state and out-of-state researchers. Grant agreements would require that the recipient offer the selected institute or the University of California, Los Angeles, to substantially participate in the funded research. The initiative would also require the recipient to pay the state 10% of all revenues derived from the sale, licensing, or any other commercial monetization of any intellectual property rights produced by the funded research. The initiative would also require recipients to purchase as many goods and services used for the research as possible from California suppliers.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)  
 

The initiative would require grant recipients to own any intellectual property created from the research, meaning employees, scientists, researchers, contractors, or anyone paid with the grant would be required to formally assign their patent or intellectual property rights to the institution receiving the funding. ## Prediction markets

*See also: [Prediction markets](/Prediction_markets "Prediction markets")*

A prediction market is a platform where users buy and sell contracts tied to the outcome of future events. The price of a contract reflects the market's estimated probability of that outcome — a contract priced at 55 cents suggests the market estimates a 55 percent chance the event occurs. Volume reflects how actively a market is being traded.[\[8\]](#cite_note-8) Unlike polls, which survey a sample of voters, prediction markets aggregate the financial stakes of individual bettors. A market with higher trading volume is generally considered more reliable than one with low volume, though prices can be influenced by large individual traders.

## Background

### Immunology and immunotherapy

Immunology is the study of the body's immune system and how it protects itself against abnormal cells or pathogens. Immunotherapy is the clinical practice of immunology, whereby researchers develop treatments to fight diseases or cancers by utilizing, stimulating, or modifying the body's own immune system. According to the Legislative Analyst's Office, there are at least 10 research centers that study immunology and immunotherapy in California.[\[9\]](#cite_note-9) 

### Voter-approved bonds for healthcare research in California

*See also: [California Proposition 71, Stem Cell Research Initiative (2004)](/California_Proposition_71,_Stem_Cell_Research_Initiative_\(2004\) "California Proposition 71, Stem Cell Research Initiative (2004)") and [California Proposition 14, Stem Cell Research Institute Bond Initiative (2020)](/California_Proposition_14,_Stem_Cell_Research_Institute_Bond_Initiative_\(2020\) "California Proposition 14, Stem Cell Research Institute Bond Initiative (2020)")*

In 2020, California voters approved [Proposition 14](/California_Proposition_14,_Stem_Cell_Research_Institute_Bond_Initiative_\(2020\) "California Proposition 14, Stem Cell Research Institute Bond Initiative (2020)") by a margin of 51% to 49% to issue $5.5 billion in general obligation bonds for the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine (CIRM), which was created to fund stem cell research. In 2004, voters approved [Proposition 71](/California_Proposition_71,_Stem_Cell_Research_Initiative_\(2004\) "California Proposition 71, Stem Cell Research Initiative (2004)"), which created CIRM, issued $3 billion in bonds to finance CIRM, and established a state constitutional right to conduct stem cell research.[\[10\]](#cite_note-initiative-10) 

The 2020 ballot initiative required CIRM to spend no more than 7.5% of the bond funds on operation costs. The remaining bond funds were to be spent on grants to entities that conduct research, trials, and programs related to stem cells, as well as start-up costs for facilities. Some of the bond funds were set to be dedicated, including $1.5 billion for research on therapies and treatments for brain and nervous system diseases, such as Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and dementia. Upwards of 1.5% of the total funds were to be spent on Community Care Centers of Excellence (CCCE), which would be sites that conduct human clinical trials, treatments, and cures. Upwards of 0.5% of the total funds were to be spent on the Shared Labs Program (SLP), which are state-funded facilities dedicated to research on human embryonic stem cells.[\[10\]](#cite_note-initiative-10)

{"type":"WebSearch","query":"CIRM California stem cell bond royalty returns Proposition 71 fiscal outcome","content":"**Proposition 71 (2004) authorized $3 billion in general obligation bonds to create and fund the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine (CIRM) for stem cell research.** The state pays principal plus interest from the General Fund. Original estimates put the total cost at about $6 billion over 30 years (roughly $200 million annually). Later reports indicated higher annual debt service (e.g., around $327 million in 2019). Prop 71 funds have been largely expended, with CIRM later receiving additional $5.5 billion via Proposition 14 (2020).[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_71,_Stem_Cell_Research_Initiative_(2004))

**Royalty returns have been modest and far below early campaign projections** (some analyses cited potential hundreds of millions to over $1 billion). Grant recipients must share licensing/commercialization revenue under CIRM IP rules (typically 15-25% of licensing revenue above a ~$500k threshold, or royalties on net commercial sales, with “blockbuster” provisions for high-revenue products). Royalties go into a dedicated Licensing Revenues and Royalties Fund (not directly to bond repayment) to help California patients afford CIRM-related treatments.[[2]](https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-hsc/division-106/part-5/chapter-3/article-1/section-125290-30/)

- First payment arrived in 2018: ~$190,000 from City of Hope.  
- By 2019, cumulative invention-related income was about $353,000.  
- A major 2022 payment of $15.6 million came from Stanford (tied to the Gilead acquisition of Forty Seven Inc., which had CIRM support). Prior cumulative royalties were only ~$557,000.  
- Subsequent amounts have been small (e.g., ~$125,000 licensing/royalty revenue in FY 2023; the royalties fund received ~$475,000–$677,000 in recent years, including interest). As of June 30, 2024, the royalties fund held about $16.8 million (mostly the Stanford payment plus interest; little spending from it yet).[[3]](https://capitolweekly.net/state-stem-cell-agencys-first-royalties-15-million-from-stanford/)

**Fiscal outcome**: Direct royalty returns represent a tiny fraction of the $3 billion principal (plus billions in interest). Broader economic analyses (some CIRM-commissioned) claim positive impacts, such as tens of thousands of jobs, ~$10 billion in economic output, and hundreds of millions in tax revenue that partially offset costs. Critics highlight that promised self-funding via royalties never materialized, no FDA-approved therapies resulted from CIRM-funded science as of the late 2010s (though many projects reached clinical trials), and there were governance/conflict-of-interest issues. CIRM has funded infrastructure, training, and research that advanced California’s regenerative medicine sector, with follow-on private investment reported in the billions. Ongoing royalties remain limited as most funded work is still pre-commercial.[[4]](https://schaeffer.usc.edu/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/The-Economic-Case-for-Public-Investment-in-Stem-Cell-Research_FINAL-1-1.pdf)

CIRM continues operations with remaining Prop 14 funds, focusing on clinical translation and patient access. {"type":"WebSearch","query":"Proposition 38 California text of law institute selection criteria Public Records Act exemption site:vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov","content":"**Proposition 38 (November 3, 2026 California General Election) is an initiative statute titled “Authorizes Bonds for Immunology Medical Research.”** It would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research (with at least $4.2 billion focused on cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s), split roughly equally between a single selected nonprofit research institute and competitive grants.[[1]](https://quickguidetoprops.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2026-11-03/38)

The official text of the proposed law appears in the California Voter Information Guide (complete-vig.pdf). Relevant excerpts on **institute selection criteria** (primarily Health & Safety Code § 130353) and the **Public Records Act exemption** (§ 130363) follow. (Text extraction from the PDF has some formatting artifacts; the official PDF is the authoritative source.)

### Institute Selection Criteria (§ 130353)
The State Department of Public Health (department) shall disburse 50% of the funds to a **single nonprofit medical research institute** selected by the department that satisfies **all** of the following criteria:

- (1) It is a medical research institute exempt from federal income taxation pursuant to Section 501(c)(3) of the Internal Revenue Code that was in existence as of January 1, 2025, and that was founded for the primary purpose of, and specializes specifically in, conducting research in the fields of immunology and immunotherapy.
- (2) It has an affiliation agreement, entered into not later than January 1, 2025, that creates an affiliation relationship with a campus of the University of California that satisfies all of the following:
  - (A) The campus has a graduate training program in immunology and immunotherapy.
  - (B) The campus has a public health care system that consists of one or more hospitals and that conducts its own clinical trials of new experimental drugs and therapies.
  - (C) The campus health care system has a hospital and clinic volume of greater than 35,000 inpatient admissions and 3,500,000 outpatient visits each year.
- (3) The institute is governed by a board of directors that is required by the institute’s bylaws, adopted not later than January 1, 2025, and by the affiliation agreement described in paragraph (2) to include multiple members who are senior-level representatives of the University of California campus that is a party to the affiliation agreement or the campus’s public health care system.
- (4) As of January 1, 2026, the institute owns or leases a site that is not less than 200,000 square feet in size and that has an intended purpose of serving as a research facility housing the institute’s research activities.
- (5) The institute agrees to conduct collaborative medical research in immunology and immunotherapy with other qualified nonprofit California medical research centers, including conducting multiinstitutional clinical trials.
- (6) The institute has identified, in the affiliation agreement described in paragraph (2), sources of funding of not less than two hundred fifty million dollars ($250,000,000) in the form of philanthropic donations or fundraising commitments.
- (7) The institute has secured financial commitments of not less than fifty million dollars ($50,000,000) to support a rapid vaccine development program and not less than fifty million dollars ($50,000,000) to support a microbiome research program.

The department shall select and enter into a funding agreement within 90 days of the chapter’s effective date (with limited ability to make the *minimum* modifications to criteria necessary if no qualifying institute is identified). The agreement is reviewed every five years for compliance. Additional provisions cover start-up loans, research standards (open scientific exchange, peer review, public oversight), and required expenditures (e.g., at least $2.1 billion of the institute’s share on cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research).[[2]](https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/complete-vig.pdf)

(Note: Reporting indicates only one institute currently appears to meet these highly specific criteria.)[[3]](https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/)

### Grant Selection Criteria (§ 130356, for the other 50% of funds)
The Advisory and Accountability Research Council shall determine which research projects (from public/nonprofit universities and institutions represented on the council) are funded, based on selection criteria and research priorities established under the chapter plus technical merits. Criteria include:
- Scientific merits of a proposal.
- Experience of the applicant in conducting methodologically sound medical research.
- Potential benefits to the health and well-being of the population.
- Other criteria as determined by the council.

Highest priority goes to projects with the greatest potential for yielding the most immediate, accessible, and affordable therapies that enhance patient access to immunotherapy treatments. Peer review panels of immunology/immunotherapy experts may be used. Grants are generally limited to California-based researchers/projects (with some collaboration exceptions). Conflict-of-interest standards based on National Academy of Sciences best practices apply.[[2]](https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/complete-vig.pdf)

### Public Records Act Exemption (§ 130363)
**(a)** Notwithstanding any other law, **the institute shall not be deemed a public agency for any purpose under state law**, including, but not limited to, Division 10 (commencing with Section 7920.000) of Title 1 of [the California Public Records Act], Article 9 (commencing with Section 11120) of Chapter 1 of Part 1 of Division 3 of Title 2 of [Bagley-Keene Open Meeting Act], and Title 9 (commencing with Section 81000) of, the Government Code [Political Reform Act].

The Political Reform Act applies to the council with specified exceptions (e.g., members may participate in certain disease-related research decisions involving themselves or family; adoption of general selection criteria/priorities is not a conflicted decision). Service on the council by UC faculty/administrators is not deemed incompatible with their UC duties.[[2]](https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/complete-vig.pdf)

For the full official text, arguments, analysis, and fiscal impact, see the complete Voter Information Guide PDF (vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/complete-vig.pdf) or the Secretary of State’s site. The measure also includes bond issuance details, intellectual property provisions, audits, a 20% Rx discount mandate for California patients on resulting products, and other requirements.","citations":["https://quickguidetoprops.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2026-11-03/38","https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/complete-vig.pdf","https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/"],"allowed_domains":null}

There are 14 measures on the state ballot, many of them dense and extremely complicated tax policies. Voters in San Francisco and Oakland will also have to weigh in on hugely impactful charter reform ballot measures that could change the future of their cities.

In this kind of environment, details matter. And, yes, your vote matters.

The San Francisco Chronicle editorial board has spent months interviewing candidates, talking to experts, fact checking campaign promises and scrutinizing the issues in every statewide contest on the ballot, along with a group of consequential races in the Bay Area. These recommendations are made by Opinion writers and editors; newsroom reporters who cover the campaigns do not participate in endorsement decisions.

###### The editorial board recommends

Why we're endorsing

Befitting the broad consensus on California’s affordability crisis, Prop 1 has no formal opposition. The measure is the product of years of legislative sausage-making and is unwieldy. But the need for more affordable housing is too desperate to wait — and Prop 1 is well-positioned to reap the benefits of the state’s new streamlining laws.

Why we're endorsing

Wouldn’t it feel great to vote for something everyone can agree will make a positive difference in the world? Prop 38 positions itself as such a balm. In fact, it’s one of the most noxious deposits on California’s political dung heap in years. It would give billions to an institute co-founded by billionaire Michael Milken, also known as the “junk bond king,” who was pardoned by Trump in 2020.

[Read the full editorial](https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php)

Why we're endorsing

California could do more to assuage concerns about election integrity. But even if you think voter fraud is a problem in California, Prop 39 would turn our elections into a never-ending lawsuit.

No one is coming to save us, and it won’t be the wealthy who suffer. California isn’t a lab rat. Voters shouldn’t allow our state to be treated like one.

[Read the full editorial](https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-40-tax-billionaire-california-22477038.php)
